title: The Arabian sky of the anwāʾ
note: Human-curated source records (UFUQ, 2026-11-05). Names and memberships follow the owner's navigation compilation (Stellarium Arabic (Ancient), CC BY-ND 4.0, cited per record, never its line arrays) checked against the owner's primary anwāʾ texts. Notes are UFUQ English paraphrases of passages read in those texts; locators point into the local text layers and are unverified against print editions. Lines are drawn by the UFUQ_TREE_V1 rule (MODERN_PEDAGOGICAL). Nothing here is culturally approved.

transliteration.rules: Article al- kept before sun letters; ʿ for ʿayn, ʾ for hamza; macrons for long vowels; dots for emphatics; tāʾ marbūṭa as -a, -at in construct; no translation of names.
transliteration.vocalization: From the vocalized source forms and IAU WGSN/Kunitzsch spellings; records marked UNVERIFIED need a philologist.

lineRule.description: Members are joined by the shortest-separation spanning tree (great-circle distance at the catalogue epoch, ties by HIP). A figure whose members include a smaller figure keeps that figure's segments. RING figures (texts describe a square or ring) also join the two ends of the tree when it is a simple path.

notes.text: Seven bright stars: four are the bier (al-naʿsh) and three are the daughters (banāt). The first daughter is al-Qāʾid, the middle one ʿAnāq and the one next to the bier al-Jawn.
A very faint star almost touching the middle daughter is al-Suhā, a famous test of sight.
Neither Banāt Naʿsh group is a lunar mansion: they never meet the moon and no rain is attributed to them. Astrologers called the groups the greater and lesser bears.

notes.text: One of the gazelles' leaps (qafazāt al-ẓibāʾ): each pair of stars looks like the hoofprints a gazelle leaves where it leaps. The story says the lion struck with its tail and the gazelles fled.

conflicts.text: Ibn Qutayba describes the leaps (also al-Qarāʾin and al-Thaʿlabiyyāt) as four stars, two clear and two faint, lying beneath Banāt Naʿsh when it is high. The compilation draws three pairs, and names each leap separately.

notes.text: The outstretched, henna-dyed hand of al-Thurayyā: five white stars in the Milky Way facing al-Ḥūt. Ibn Qutayba quotes a Syrian poet, al-Ḥiṣnī, who knew the stars well.
The same five stars can be read as the hump of al-Nāqa.
Ibn Kunāsa: when Saʿd al-Dhābiḥ sets at dawn, the head of al-Ḥūt marks the qibla (from Iraq), "and it is bridled to al-Kaff al-Khaḍīb".

conflicts.text: Ibn ʿĀṣim's text (as read locally) calls al-Kaff al-Khaḍīb faint stars of irregular arrangement, unlike Ibn Qutayba's five white stars; check the reading against a scan.

relationships.statement: al-Farqadān are the two leading bier stars of the lesser Banāt Naʿsh; al-Jady is the last daughter of the same seven-star group, so the group leads from the bright pair to al-Jady.
relationships.context: OLD_ARABIAN description; the drawn path is a UFUQ teaching aid

relationships.statement: The greater Banāt Naʿsh lies near the lesser group (whose bier stars are al-Farqadān).
relationships.context: OLD_ARABIAN description. The modern "pointer" rule (Merak to Dubhe to Polaris) is not stated in the anwāʾ texts read here and would be MODERN_PEDAGOGICAL

relationships.statement: al-Abyaḍ, at the edge of the Milky Way, faces al-Jady about a spear's length away.
relationships.context: OLD_ARABIAN description; a candidate bridge from the Cassiopeia-Cepheus region to al-Jady

relationships.statement: The small stars of al-Shāʾ lie between al-Qurḥa and al-Jady; al-Rāʿī is the brightest of them.
relationships.context: OLD_ARABIAN description; candidate stepping stones towards al-Jady

relationships.statement: al-Qarn, two stars with al-Qurḥa below them, stand beside al-Jady on its eastern side.
The five stars of al-Kaff al-Khaḍīb lie in the Milky Way facing al-Ḥūt; Ibn Kunāsa says the head of al-Ḥūt is "bridled" to al-Kaff al-Khaḍīb.
al-Ḥurrān (al-Dhiʾbān) lie between al-ʿAwāʾidh and al-Farqadān: a path from al-ʿAwāʾidh through al-Dhiʾbān to al-Farqadān and al-Jady.
al-ʿAwāʾidh lie to the left of al-Nasr al-Wāqiʿ, between it and Banāt Naʿsh.
Between al-Farqadān and Banāt Naʿsh lie stars called al-Ḥayya (the snake).
relationships.context: OLD_ARABIAN description; al-Ḥayya itself is not yet identified in this curation

relationships.statement: The red al-Dhīkh lies above al-Ḍibāʿ, between Banāt Naʿsh and al-Nasr al-Wāqiʿ.
al-Fawāris lie behind al-Nasr al-Wāqiʿ, with al-Ridf just behind them.
The ring of al-Fakka lies behind al-Simāk al-Rāmiḥ; the two nasaqs start near al-Fakka.
The northern nasaq runs from near al-Fakka to al-Nasr al-Wāqiʿ.
Kabid al-Asad is a red star between al-ʿAwwāʾ and Banāt Naʿsh.
relationships.context: OLD_ARABIAN description; identification of the star is disputed

relationships.statement: The gazelles' leaps lie beneath Banāt Naʿsh when it is high.
al-ʿAyyūq rises when al-Thurayyā rises and lies behind it, nearer the pole; al-Aʿlām follow it.
al-Dabarān follows al-Thurayyā across the sky; its name comes from this following.
Look for al-Buṭayn between al-Sharaṭān and al-Thurayyā.
al-Ghafr lies between al-Simāk al-Aʿzal and al-Zubānā.
al-ʿUdhra lies below al-Shiʿrā al-ʿAbūr; when al-ʿUdhra culminates, Suhayl is below it: a southern path from al-Jawzāʾ through al-ʿAbūr and al-ʿUdhra to Suhayl.

Travelling north (to Syria) keep al-Jady and Banāt Naʿsh ahead and Suhayl behind; travelling south (to Yemen) the reverse; travelling east face the mansions with al-Jady on the left and the Shiʿrās and Suhayl on the right; west the reverse.
relationships.context: Historical practice from Iraq; directions are general (north/south/east/west), valid in principle anywhere north of the equator

relationships.statement: For Iraq, the qibla is faced with al-Jady against the right shoulder or the back of the neck.
relationships.context: Historical, region-specific (Iraq). Not valid for UMPSA Pekan; a UFUQ lesson must use the computed modern Qibla bearing

relationships.statement: When al-Qurḥa rises, one faces the qibla of al-Kūfa.
Ibn Kunāsa: when a mansion sets at dawn, the seventh mansion after it marks the qibla (for example al-Sharaṭān setting gives al-Dhirāʿ); the scorpion's mansions set together and break the count.
Suhayl rises on the left of someone facing the qibla of Iraq.
The rising point of al-Simāk al-Aʿzal divides the stars into northern (shaʾmiya) and southern (yamāniya).
